questions.body: What defines a Functional Interface in Java, and what is the role of the `@FunctionalInterface` annotation?
questions.keyPoints: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM). The annotation causes a compile-time error if the SAM condition is violated.

options.text: An interface with exactly one abstract method (Single Abstract Method); the annotation instructs the compiler to verify this condition.
options.explanation: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (can have multiple default and static methods). The @FunctionalInterface annotation enforces this at compile time.

options.text: An interface that extends java.lang.Runnable and contains no methods at all.
options.explanation: Runnable has run(); marker interfaces have no methods, but functional interfaces require exactly one abstract method.

options.text: An interface whose methods can only be executed concurrently on background worker threads.
options.explanation: Functional interfaces define lambda target types; execution model depends on how the method is called.

options.text: An interface that cannot define any default or static methods.
options.explanation: Functional interfaces can define any number of default and static methods, as long as there is only one abstract method.

questions.body: Which standard functional interface from `java.util.function` takes an input argument of type `T` and returns a `boolean`?
questions.keyPoints: Predicate<T> accepts an argument of type T and returns a boolean value via test(T t).

options.text: Predicate<T>
options.explanation: Predicate<T> defines 'boolean test(T t)'. Function<T, R> returns R, Consumer<T> returns void, and Supplier<T> takes no arguments and returns T.

options.text: Consumer<T>
options.explanation: Consumer<T> defines 'void accept(T t)', performing side effects without returning a value.

options.text: Function<T, R>
options.explanation: Function<T, R> defines 'R apply(T t)', mapping an input T to an arbitrary return type R.

options.text: Supplier<T>
options.explanation: Supplier<T> defines 'T get()', taking no input parameters.

questions.subtopic: Default and Static Methods in Interfaces
questions.body: If class `C` implements two interfaces `A` and `B`, and both define a default method with the exact same signature `void log()`, what happens at compile time?
questions.keyPoints: The compiler issues an error due to the diamond problem; class C must explicitly override log() and resolve the conflict.

options.text: A compilation error occurs; class C must explicitly override log() and disambiguate (e.g., A.super.log() or its own logic).
options.explanation: Java enforces explicit conflict resolution when multiple interfaces provide conflicting default method implementations with identical signatures.

options.text: The compiler automatically picks the method from the interface declared first in the implements clause.
options.explanation: Java does not resolve default method conflicts based on declaration order in the implements list.

options.text: The JVM randomly selects one implementation at runtime.
options.explanation: Java is statically typed and rejects this at compile time.

options.text: Both methods execute sequentially at runtime whenever log() is called.
options.explanation: Both methods cannot execute implicitly; explicit resolution in the implementing class is required.

questions.body: Which lambda expression is exactly equivalent to the method reference `String::compareToIgnoreCase`?
questions.keyPoints: A method reference to an instance method of an arbitrary object of a particular type takes the first parameter as the target object.

options.text: (s1, s2) -> s1.compareToIgnoreCase(s2)
options.explanation: String::compareToIgnoreCase refers to an instance method of an arbitrary object of type String. In a BiFunction context, the first argument becomes the target: s1.compareToIgnoreCase(s2).

options.text: s -> s.compareToIgnoreCase(s)
options.explanation: compareToIgnoreCase requires an argument to compare against.

options.text: () -> String.compareToIgnoreCase()
options.explanation: compareToIgnoreCase is not a static zero-argument method on String.

options.text: s -> new String(s).compareToIgnoreCase()
options.explanation: This would use constructor reference String::new, not method reference.

questions.body: Why is invoking `optional.get()` without first calling `optional.isPresent()` considered an anti-pattern in Java?
questions.keyPoints: optional.get() throws NoSuchElementException if the value is empty, nullifying the safety benefits of Optional.

options.text: It throws a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty, defeating the primary purpose of Optional to eliminate unexpected runtime exceptions.
options.explanation: Calling get() blindly reproduces the exact risk of NullPointerException (as NoSuchElementException). Idiomatic usage uses orElse(), orElseGet(), or map().

options.text: It forces an immediate garbage collection cycle on the referenced object.
options.explanation: Optional methods have no special interaction with GC.

options.text: It synchronizes the entire thread pool on the Optional's internal lock.
options.explanation: Optional is a simple value wrapper with no concurrency locking.

options.text: It is deprecated and fails to compile starting in Java 11.
options.explanation: get() is not deprecated (though orElseThrow() is preferred as clearer syntax).

questions.body: What is the crucial performance difference between `optional.orElse(computeDefault())` and `optional.orElseGet(() -> computeDefault())`?
questions.keyPoints: orElse evaluates its argument eagerly every time; orElseGet takes a Supplier and evaluates lazily only when the Optional is empty.

options.text: orElse evaluates computeDefault() eagerly even if the Optional already has a value; orElseGet evaluates computeDefault() lazily only if the Optional is empty.
options.explanation: Because orElse takes a value parameter, Java evaluates arguments before method invocation. orElseGet takes a Supplier<T>, deferring execution until needed.

options.text: orElse runs asynchronously on a worker thread, while orElseGet runs synchronously on the main thread.
options.explanation: Both run synchronously on the calling thread.

options.text: orElse throws an exception if computeDefault() returns null, while orElseGet allows null.
options.explanation: Both return null if the fallback evaluates to null (though returning null from orElseGet is discouraged).

options.text: There is no difference; the Java JIT compiler inlines and optimizes them identically.
options.explanation: The semantic difference is evaluation timing: eager vs lazy evaluation.

questions.keyPoints: Streams are lazily evaluated; intermediate operations like map() do not execute without a terminal operation.

options.text: Streams are evaluated lazily; intermediate operations like map() do not execute until a terminal operation (like forEach, collect, count) is invoked.
options.explanation: Stream pipelines only process elements when a terminal operation triggers the pipeline pull mechanism.

options.text: System.out is disabled inside lambda expressions by the Java runtime security manager.
options.explanation: Lambdas have full standard access to System.out.

options.text: Stream.of creates an empty stream unless passed an array variable reference.
options.explanation: Stream.of("a", "b", "c") creates a valid 3-element stream.

options.text: The elements are buffered in Metaspace and only printed when the JVM shuts down.
options.explanation: Streams do not buffer into Metaspace.

questions.body: When transforming data in a Java Stream, when should you use `flatMap` instead of `map`?
questions.keyPoints: flatMap is used when the mapping function returns a Stream for each element, flattening a Stream<Stream<T>> into Stream<T>.

options.text: When each input element maps to a Stream of elements (1-to-many), and you want to flatten the resulting Stream of Streams into a single combined Stream.
options.explanation: map transforms T -> R (yielding Stream<R>). When T maps to Stream<R>, map yields Stream<Stream<R>>, whereas flatMap flattens the contents into Stream<R>.

options.text: When you want to execute the mapping operation concurrently across multiple CPU threads.
options.explanation: Parallel execution is controlled by stream.parallel(), not flatMap.

options.text: When you need to filter out null elements before applying a transformation.
options.explanation: Null filtering is handled by filter(Objects::nonNull).

options.text: When transforming primitive types (int, long, double) to their corresponding wrapper objects.
options.explanation: Boxing is handled by .boxed() or mapToObj().

questions.body: Which collector expression groups a `List<Employee>` by department name and computes the total count of employees in each department?
questions.keyPoints: Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, Collectors.counting()) groups by department and counts elements.

options.text: Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, Collectors.counting())
options.explanation: groupingBy takes a classification function and an optional downstream collector; Collectors.counting() aggregates the count of elements in each bucket into a Map<String, Long>.

options.text: Collectors.partitioningBy(Employee::getDepartment, Collectors.summingInt())
options.explanation: partitioningBy requires a Predicate returning boolean, not a department name String.

options.text: Collectors.toMap(Employee::getDepartment, Employee::count)
options.explanation: toMap throws IllegalStateException on duplicate keys unless a merge function is provided.

options.text: Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, Collectors.toList())
options.explanation: groupingBy with toList() yields Map<String, List<Employee>>, not the count.

questions.body: What happens if you invoke a terminal operation twice on the exact same `Stream` instance in Java?
questions.keyPoints: Streams are single-use; attempting to consume a stream that has already been operated upon or closed throws IllegalStateException.

options.text: An IllegalStateException is thrown indicating that the stream has already been operated upon or closed.
options.explanation: Streams cannot be reused once a terminal operation has been executed. A new stream must be created from the source collection.

options.text: The stream resets its internal cursor and iterates through the data source a second time.
options.explanation: Java streams do not support rewinding or resetting.

options.text: The second terminal operation returns an empty collection or 0 without error.
options.explanation: It does not silently return empty; it throws an IllegalStateException.

options.text: A ConcurrentModificationException is thrown by the backing collection.
options.explanation: ConcurrentModificationException occurs when mutating a collection while iterating, not from stream reuse.

questions.body: By default, which thread pool executes tasks when you invoke `collection.parallelStream()`?
questions.keyPoints: Parallel streams run on the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool() by default.

options.text: The JVM-wide shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), whose parallelism defaults to Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1.
options.explanation: All parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool across the entire JVM. Running blocking I/O on parallel streams can starve other components sharing this pool.

options.text: A freshly allocated Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10) created exclusively for that stream pipeline.
options.explanation: A new thread pool is not created per stream.

options.text: The operating system kernel thread dispatch queue directly.
options.explanation: Java manages thread execution through the ForkJoinPool abstraction.

options.text: The single main application thread via non-blocking event loops.
options.explanation: Parallel streams actively use multiple worker threads from the common pool.

questions.body: Why is the modern `java.time` API (e.g. `LocalDate`, `Instant`, `ZonedDateTime`) superior to the legacy `java.util.Date` and `Calendar`?
questions.keyPoints: java.time classes are immutable and thread-safe, have clear separation of concerns, and use intuitive 1-based months.

options.text: java.time classes are immutable and thread-safe, separate machine time (Instant) from human date/time, and use 1-based indexing for months.
options.explanation: Legacy Date/Calendar classes are mutable and notoriously thread-unsafe (SimpleDateFormat causes concurrency bugs). java.time is strictly immutable and thread-safe.

options.text: java.time calculates solar time by querying atomic clocks over NTP on every call.
options.explanation: It reads system time via Clock without network calls.

options.text: java.time stores timestamps directly in CPU hardware registers for zero allocation.
options.explanation: java.time classes are standard immutable heap objects.

options.text: java.time deprecates time zone handling to prevent daylight saving errors.
options.explanation: ZonedDateTime and ZoneId provide comprehensive, robust timezone and DST handling.

questions.body: In a `module-info.java` file, what is the effect of the directive `exports com.example.service;`?
questions.keyPoints: exports makes public types in the specified package accessible to other modules at compile-time and runtime.

options.text: It makes all public types and members in com.example.service accessible to other modules at compile-time and runtime.
options.explanation: The exports directive makes the public API of that package accessible to other modules that 'require' this module. Unexported packages remain encapsulated even if public.

options.text: It downloads external Maven dependencies needed by com.example.service.
options.explanation: JPMS is an in-JDK module system, not a Maven dependency manager.

options.text: It exposes private fields and methods to reflection for Spring and Jackson.
options.explanation: Deep reflection access is granted using the 'opens' directive, not 'exports'.

options.text: It compiles com.example.service into a native DLL/SO binary.
options.explanation: JPMS does not compile to native shared libraries.

questions.body: Where is the `var` keyword permitted in Java 10+, and what does it do?
questions.keyPoints: var is only allowed for local variables with initializers; type is inferred at compile-time, not dynamic at runtime.

options.text: Only for local variables with initializers; the compiler infers the static type at compile-time, preserving strict static typing.
options.explanation: var cannot be used for method parameters, return types, or class fields. It is purely compile-time static type inference with zero runtime dynamic typing overhead.

options.text: Anywhere in Java code, turning Java into a dynamically typed language like JavaScript.
options.explanation: Java remains strongly and statically typed; var is purely syntactic inference.

options.text: Only for method return types to allow multiple return types.
options.explanation: var is explicitly prohibited as a method return type.

options.text: As a class field modifier to enable lazy property initialization.
options.explanation: var cannot be used for instance or static fields.

questions.body: What does the Java compiler automatically generate when you declare `public record Point(int x, int y) {}`?
questions.keyPoints: Records generate private final fields, a canonical constructor, getters (x(), y()), equals(), hashCode(), and toString().

options.text: Private final fields, a canonical constructor, public accessor methods x() and y(), and implementations of equals(), hashCode(), and toString().
options.explanation: Records are immutable data carriers where the compiler synthesizes final fields, constructor, accessors (named without 'get'), and value-based equals/hashCode/toString.

options.text: A mutable JavaBean with getX(), setX(), getY(), and setY() methods.
options.explanation: Record fields are final and have no setters.

options.text: An interface that must be implemented by database entity classes.
options.explanation: A record is a concrete final class extending java.lang.Record.

options.text: A thread-safe singleton object cached in the String constant pool.
options.explanation: Records instantiate standard objects, not singletons.

questions.body: What is the primary architectural purpose of Sealed Classes introduced in Java 17?
questions.keyPoints: Sealed classes restrict which classes or interfaces may extend or implement them using the permits clause.

options.text: To restrict which classes or interfaces may extend or implement them using the permits clause, enabling exhaustive compile-time pattern matching.
options.explanation: Sealed classes declare permitted subclasses via 'permits', allowing closed class hierarchies where the compiler knows all possible subtypes and enforces exhaustive switch matching without a default branch.

options.text: To encrypt compiled class files with AES-256 so they cannot be decompiled.
options.explanation: Sealed classes are an OOP language design construct, not bytecode cryptography.

options.text: To prevent classes from calling methods in the java.net package.
options.explanation: This refers to sandboxing or security policies, not sealed classes.

options.text: To guarantee that all instances are automatically serialized to JSON across HTTP boundaries.
options.explanation: Serialization is independent of sealed hierarchies.

questions.body: How does pattern matching for `instanceof` (Java 16) improve safety and boilerplate code?
questions.keyPoints: Pattern matching combines type testing and casting into a single atomic expression: if (obj instanceof String s).

options.text: It combines type test and casting into a single construct: if (obj instanceof String s), introducing a scoped variable s without explicit casts.
options.explanation: Instead of checking 'if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; }', pattern matching allows 'if (obj instanceof String s)', eliminating repetitive casts and casting errors.

options.text: It converts runtime polymorphism into compile-time C macros.
options.explanation: Java has no preprocessor or C macros.

options.text: It allows matching against arbitrary regular expressions inside switch statements.
options.explanation: Pattern matching in Java refers to type and deconstruction patterns, not regex strings.

options.text: It prevents ClassCastException by returning null whenever a cast is invalid.
options.explanation: Pattern matching introduces a binding variable conditionally if the test evaluates to true.

questions.body: What are Java Text Blocks (triple quotes `"""`), and how do they handle indentation?
questions.keyPoints: Text blocks provide multi-line string literals and automatically strip incidental leading white space using stripIndent().

options.text: Multi-line string literals that automatically strip common incidental leading indentation while preserving intentional formatting.
options.explanation: Text blocks strip incidental leading whitespace common to all lines, eliminating cumbersome + concatenations and escaped \n characters.

options.text: Binary memory buffers that bypass JVM UTF-16 encoding to store ASCII characters.
options.explanation: Text blocks produce standard java.lang.String objects.

options.text: Syntax for writing inline Python or SQL scripts that execute directly in kernel space.
options.explanation: Text blocks are purely string literals in Java syntax.

options.text: Special HTML templates that automatically escape XSS script tags at compile time.
options.explanation: Text blocks do not perform HTML sanitation.

questions.subtopic: Java 21 Pattern Matching with Record Deconstruction
questions.body: Given `record Point(int x, int y) {}`, how does record pattern matching simplify destructuring in Java 21?
questions.keyPoints: Record patterns deconstruct records into component variables directly in instanceof or switch: if (obj instanceof Point(int x, int y)).

options.text: It allows matching and extracting record components directly: if (obj instanceof Point(int x, int y)), extracting x and y without accessor method calls.
options.explanation: Record patterns combine type matching with component deconstruction, binding the inner components directly to variables for immediate use.

options.text: It allows records to mutate their final fields directly within switch expressions.
options.explanation: Record fields are always immutable and final.

options.text: It converts records into JSON strings automatically inside SQL queries.
options.explanation: Pattern matching does not perform SQL serialization.

options.text: It destroys the object from the heap immediately upon extraction.
options.explanation: Deconstruction extracts component values; heap objects remain until GC cleans them.

questions.body: Why is `collect()` preferred over `reduce()` when accumulating elements into a mutable container like an `ArrayList` in a Java Stream?
questions.keyPoints: collect() performs mutable reduction by mutating a single container; reduce() is intended for immutable values and requires copying the entire collection on each step.

options.text: collect() performs mutable reduction by accumulating into a shared container, whereas reduce() requires creating a new container on every element, causing O(N^2) copying overhead.
options.explanation: reduce() is designed for functional immutable value combining. Accumulating into collections via reduce requires creating and copying whole lists at each step. collect() uses a Supplier, Accumulator, and Combiner for efficient mutable reduction.

options.text: reduce() is deprecated in Java 17 and removed in Java 21.
options.explanation: reduce() is not deprecated; it is the standard fold operation for immutable values.

options.text: collect() cannot be executed in parallel, preventing race conditions.
options.explanation: collect() fully supports parallel execution via combiner functions.

options.text: reduce() only works on streams of primitive numbers (IntStream, LongStream).
options.explanation: Stream<T> provides three overloads of reduce() for arbitrary object streams.
